final_answer:
Antibiotic resistance arises through the evolutionary process of natural selection. When antibiotics are introduced into an environment, they exert selective pressure on bacterial populations. Bacteria that possess genetic mutations conferring resistance to the antibiotic are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing on their resistance traits to subsequent generations. Over time, this leads to an increase in the proportion of resistant bacteria within the population.

Overprescription of antibiotics accelerates this process by increasing the frequency and duration of exposure of bacterial populations to antibiotics. This heightened exposure intensifies selective pressure, allowing resistant strains to thrive more rapidly. Additionally, the unnecessary use of antibiotics can lead to the proliferation of resistance genes through horizontal gene transfer, where bacteria exchange genetic material, including resistance genes, across species. This mechanism further spreads resistance traits within microbial communities. Thus, overprescription not only favors the survival of resistant bacteria but also facilitates the dissemination of resistance, making infections harder to treat and reducing the effectiveness of antibiotics overall.
